notes: Mentmore Towers enabling development JR; Forbes J dismissed all three grounds and exercised discretion on s106 undertakings.

enrichment.short_title: Davey v Aylesbury Vale: judicial review of Mentmore Towers hotel enabling development
key_facts: Aylesbury Vale District Council granted detailed planning permission and listed building consent to convert Grade I Mentmore Towers into a 101-room luxury hotel with a three-storey Derby Wing extension.
Claimant David Davey, owner of adjoining Cheddington Lodge, challenged the permission on enabling development, green travel plan and helicopter restriction grounds.
English Heritage did not object on heritage grounds but the proposal conflicted with countryside policies; Knight Frank advised the council on viability and enabling development.
After the claim was issued Mentmore executed a unilateral section 106 undertaking prohibiting helicopter landings and committing to a green travel plan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning permission and listed building approval granted after extended Development Control Committee consideration.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all three grounds; enabling development approach held rational, traffic and helicopter challenges failed or were academic given the section 106 undertaking.
enrichment.ratio: Weight given to English Heritage enabling development guidance is a matter of planning judgment for the local authority; where a section 106 undertaking adequately addresses travel plan and helicopter concerns, relief may be refused in the court's discretion even if a substantive ground were made out.
legal_issues: Whether officers fairly advised members on English Heritage enabling development policy and Knight Frank's report
Whether failure to require a green travel plan under PPG 13 vitiated the permission
Whether the Head of Planning unlawfully omitted a helicopter restriction condition
Whether section 106 undertakings given after the claim could defeat EIA-related relief
linked_authorities: Tesco Stores Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment [1995] 2 All ER 636
Berkeley v Secretary of State for the Environment [2001] 2 AC 603
Simplex v Secretary of State for the Environment and St Albans DC [1988] 57 P & CR 306

confidence.notes: Three grounds, factual background and final dismissal are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Interlocutory ECJ reference application in O2 v H3G comparative advertising dispute; reference declined as premature.

enrichment.short_title: O2 v Hutchison 3G: premature Article 234 reference on bubble mark infringement
key_facts: O2 sued H3G over a 20-second TV comparative advertisement using bubble imagery alongside the O2 sign to compare pay-as-you-go call costs.
O2 abandoned word mark and passing off claims but pursued infringement of twelve registered bubble device marks and sought twelve preliminary rulings under Article 234.
H3G counterclaimed for invalidity of the bubble marks on bad faith and lack of distinctive character grounds.
O2 argued an early ECJ reference would eliminate or reduce extensive factual inquiry at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for a pre-trial reference to the European Court of Justice under Article 234 EC Treaty.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; twelve proposed questions held premature because validity, identification of the relevant sign and factual findings must precede any reference.
enrichment.ratio: A national court may refer before trial but should not do so when it cannot yet say answers are necessary to give judgment; questions framed with subordinate clauses depending on prior findings of fact are contingent and premature, and delay may prejudice trial evidence.
legal_issues: Whether twelve trade mark and comparative advertising questions should be referred before trial
Whether section 10(6) Trade Marks Act 1994 is void for incomplete harmonisation
Whether bubble marks lack distinctive character or were applied for in bad faith
What constitutes the relevant sign in a moving image advertisement
linked_authorities: Irish Creamery Milk Suppliers Association v Ireland [1981] ECR 735
SA Societe LTJ Diffusion v SA Sadas [2003] ECR I-2799
Zino Davidoff SA v A & G Imports Ltd [2001] ECR I-8691

confidence.notes: Twelve questions and reasons for declining reference are clearly set out though appendix questions are not reproduced in full.

notes: GMC Health Committee appeal; Stanley Burnton J quashed serious impairment finding for inadequate reasons and weak evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Cullen v GMC: appeal against fitness-to-practise impairment finding
key_facts: Dr Cullen, a 72-year-old retired GP working as an RAF locum, faced GMC concerns after colleagues reported slow comprehension, prescribing errors and behavioural problems at RAF Halton.
Psychiatric assessments were divided: Dr Katz suspected mild cognitive disorder while Professors Pitt and Trimble found no mental disorder or serious impairment.
The Health Committee preferred Dr Katz's evidence, found fitness seriously impaired by ICD-10 F06.7 mild cognitive disorder and imposed stringent registration conditions.
Dr Cullen appealed on insufficiency of evidence, irrational preference for Dr Katz and inadequate reasons for rejecting contrary expert opinion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under the Medical Act 1983 against a GMC Health Committee determination on fitness to practise.
enrichment.outcome: Committee decision quashed and case remitted to a differently constituted Health Committee; further medical reports including MRI or EEG suggested.
enrichment.ratio: Where a disciplinary tribunal rejects the preponderance of unchallenged expert evidence in favour of a minority view, it must explain why; on a full merits appeal the court may interfere if the evidence was insufficient to find fitness seriously impaired or reasons were inadequate.
legal_issues: Meaning of fitness to practise being seriously impaired under section 37
Whether the Committee irrationally preferred Dr Katz's opinion
Adequacy of reasons where majority expert evidence was rejected
Whether the appeal is limited to questions of law or permits full merits review
linked_authorities: Threlfall v General Optical Council [2004] EWHC 2683 (Admin)
Ghosh v General Medical Council [2001] UKPC 29

confidence.notes: Detailed medical evidence, Committee reasons and quashing order are fully analysed.

notes: Permission to appeal refused on brickwork sub-contract terms; Rix LJ rejects novel duty to highlight term changes.

enrichment.short_title: Tombs v Wilson Connolly: which sub-contract terms governed brickwork at Thetford
key_facts: Sub-contractor Tombs signed Wilson Connolly's new Labour Sub-Contract Short Form in October 2001, expressly accepting clauses 28, 29, 32 and 36 in separate 42-term conditions.
Wilson Connolly later issued unsigned sub-contract orders on the old form containing 20 terms including a defect rectification clause favourable to Tombs.
The TCC held the parties contracted on the new terms and that post-contract old-form orders did not vary the agreement.
Tombs sought permission to appeal on the novel proposition that a proposer must draw attention to changes between old and new terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from a Technology and Construction Court preliminary issue decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no real prospect of success on incorporation of new terms or variation by subsequent orders.
enrichment.ratio: Where a sub-contractor signs a written contract incorporating identified terms present when he signed, he is bound; a later document submitted after contract formation does not vary terms without acceptance, and there is no general duty to highlight contractual changes to a previous contracting partner.
legal_issues: Whether the sub-contract was made on new or old terms and conditions
Whether unsigned subsequent order forms varied the signed contract
Whether a party proposing new terms must draw the other's attention to changes from prior terms
linked_authorities: Circle Freight International Ltd v Medeast Gulf Exports Ltd [1988] 2 Lloyd's Rep 427

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue findings and refusal of permission are clearly reasoned on established contract principles.

notes: Strike-out of similar-fact Greek shipping families pleading in Springwell GKO notes litigation; Gloster J applies O'Brien test.

enrichment.short_title: JP Morgan Chase v Springwell: strike-out of similar-fact evidence from other Greek families
key_facts: Springwell, a Polemis family shipping investment company, lost heavily on Russian GKO-linked notes sold by Chase entities before the August 1998 Russian moratorium.
Springwell pleaded that Justin Atkinson of Chase gave unsuitable emerging-market investment advice and sought to rely on experiences of other Greek shipping families as similar-fact evidence.
Chase contended the relationship was execution-only counterparty dealing, not advisory, and applied to strike out paragraphs 190-193 of the defence.
Recorded telephone conversations between Atkinson and Adam Polemis were the primary evidence of what was said to Springwell.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application to strike out parts of the amended defence and counterclaim before a major Commercial Court trial.
enrichment.outcome: Paragraphs 190-193 struck out; similar-fact evidence from Kollakis, Kedros, Afentakis and Diamantides families held inadmissible and excluded in the court's discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Similar-fact evidence of what Chase said to other Greek shipping clients is not logically probative of causation or the advisory nature of its relationship with Springwell; even if marginally relevant, probative value is outweighed by cost, complexity and case-management prejudice under CPR Part 1.
legal_issues: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence under O'Brien v Chief Constable of South Wales Police
Whether other Greek families' experiences prove an advisory relationship or causation of Springwell's Russian exposure
Exercise of discretion to exclude admissible similar-fact evidence under CPR 32.1(2)
linked_authorities: O'Brien v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2003] EWCA Civ 1058
Thorpe v Chief Constable of Greater Manchester Police [1989] 1 WLR 665

confidence.notes: Two-stage O'Brien analysis and case-management reasoning are explicit and detailed.

notes: Mortgagee sale to connected BES company appeal; Court of Appeal ordered retrial applying Tse Kwong Lam.

enrichment.short_title: Bradford & Bingley v Ross: mortgagee sale to connected Homes for Tenants company
key_facts: Bradford & Bingley repossessed Mr Ross's mortgaged property in Rochdale in 1992 and sold it in July 1993 for £46,000, leaving a £29,069 shortfall claimed ten years later.
The purchaser was Homes for Tenants 4 Plc, a business expansion scheme vehicle connected to the building society, not an arm's length buyer.
The county court judge found no negligence in marketing but was not told the sale was to a connected company and applied the ordinary borrower-burden approach.
Fresh evidence on appeal showed the BES structure and that the expert valued the property at £50,000 in August 1993.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court money judgment on mortgage shortfall after repossession and sale.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment set aside and case remitted for retrial before a judge with Chancery experience on connected-party sale principles.
enrichment.ratio: Where a mortgagee sells to a company in which it has an interest, it must prove the sale was in good faith and that reasonable precautions were taken to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable; the burden lies on the mortgagee and failure to disclose the connected sale vitiates the trial.
legal_issues: Whether the mortgagee breached its duty when selling to a connected BES company
Burden and standard of proof on mortgagee sales to associated undertakings
Whether fresh evidence on connected sale should be admitted on appeal
Whether abuse of process should bar recovery without retrial
linked_authorities: Tse Kwong Lam v Wong Chit Sen [1983] 1 WLR 1349
Mortgage Express v Mardner [2004] EWCA Civ 1859

confidence.notes: Connected sale issue, Tse Kwong Lam application and retrial order are clearly reasoned.

notes: Macaulay Hall final account trial; Jackson J awards £32,854 and gives TCC costs guidance.

enrichment.short_title: Machenair v Gill: final account on Leeds university refurbishment sub-sub-contract

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Machenair carried out mechanical works at Macaulay Hall for Gill under labour-only purchase orders totalling about £54,000.
The project suffered delays from late IPS installation, late water heater delivery and numerous undocumented variations.
Gill sought to set off £14,000 delay damages and contra charges; Machenair claimed about £91,000 on its third final account version.
Gill's standard purchase conditions were not incorporated; variations were valued at 110% mark-up on time costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court Leeds on final account and counterclaim after failed negotiations.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Machenair totalling £32,854 including Wildlife Trust balance; variations £24,411; delay counterclaim failed; £500 allowed for rubbish clearance.
enrichment.ratio: A labour-only sub-sub-contractor completing within a reasonable time despite delays caused by others and extensive variations is not liable for main contractor delay damages; section 111 bars set-off but not freestanding counterclaims; Gill's conditions were not incorporated by a faxed purchase order reference.
legal_issues: Whether Gill's standard conditions were incorporated into the sub-sub-contract
Valuation of 42 variation items and appropriate mark-up
Whether Machenair delayed completion and owed delay damages
Whether section 111 barred Gill's counterclaim for set-off

confidence.notes: Item-by-item variation awards and counterclaim disposals are detailed though interest was reserved.

notes: Default judgment for Somali bereavement damages; Treacy J awards £10,000 under Fatal Accidents Act.

enrichment.short_title: Abdullah v Yusuf: default judgment for bereavement after Somalia killing
key_facts: Ahmed Mahmood, a British citizen and accountant, was shot dead in Kala-Beyr, Puntland, Somalia on 17 August 2002 after a political dispute with Colonel Abdullahi Yusuf.
Armed men from Yusuf's convoy pursued and killed Mahmood; the defendant was Puntland president and head of an armed militia though not shown to have fired the shots.
The Master struck out the defence for failure to serve documents and the defendant did not appear at the assessment hearing.
Dependency and exemplary damages claims failed for lack of evidence; only statutory bereavement damages were awarded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Assessment of damages after default judgment following jurisdictional ruling and unless order compliance failure.
enrichment.outcome: Defence struck out; judgment for £10,000 bereavement damages under section 1(1)(a) Fatal Accidents Act 1976 and summary costs assessed at £20,000 less £5,000 paid.
enrichment.ratio: An English court may adjudicate and award statutory bereavement damages where jurisdiction is established and the defendant defaults; loss of dependency requires sufficient evidence of pecuniary loss and exemplary damages are unavailable on a Fatal Accidents Act claim without the estate as party.
legal_issues: Jurisdiction of English courts over extraterritorial killing in Somalia
Quantum of bereavement damages under the 1976 Act post-April 2002
Whether loss of dependency and exemplary damages are recoverable
Summary costs assessment where enforcement abroad is unlikely

confidence.notes: Default procedure and limited award are clear though underlying killing facts rely partly on pleaded and country-report material.

notes: ASBO pre-application consultation case stated appeal; Waller LJ holds no Article 6 or 8 right to be heard beforehand.

enrichment.short_title: Wareham v Purbeck: no human rights right to consultation before ASBO application
key_facts: Purbeck District Council held an anti-social behaviour case conference in December 2003 and decided to apply for an ASBO against Carl Wareham, then 19.
Wareham was not invited to participate before the decision; he received notice of the meeting outcome and later contested the application at a full magistrates' court hearing.
A five-year ASBO was made prohibiting harassment and restricting entry to named areas and association with specified individuals in Dorset.
Wareham appealed by case stated arguing Articles 6 and 8 required consultation or a hearing before the council decided to apply.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from a magistrates' court ruling rejecting a human rights challenge to pre-application ASBO procedures.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no Article 6 or 8 right to be consulted or heard before an authority decides to apply for an ASBO; full hearing provides sufficient protection.
enrichment.ratio: The decision to apply for an ASBO is not itself an interference with Article 8 rights; interference occurs only if an order is made, and the defendant's fair trial rights under Article 6 are satisfied at the magistrates' court hearing without prior consultation.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 requires consultation before an ASBO application is made
Whether Article 6 fair trial rights extend to pre-litigation ASBO decision-making
Analogy with care proceedings procedural protection under Article 8
Whether high ASBO grant rates indicate inadequate court scrutiny
linked_authorities: R (McCann) v Crown Court at Manchester [2002] UKHL 39
Re L (Care: Assessment: Fair Trial) [2002] EWHC 1379 (Fam)

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, case conference facts and Article 6/8 conclusions are clearly stated.

notes: Murder appeal on s23/26 hearsay; Court of Appeal upholds reading intimidated witnesses' statements under Article 6.

enrichment.short_title: R v Sellick: hearsay statements of intimidated witnesses and Article 6 fairness
key_facts: Carlo and Santino Sellick were convicted of murdering Paul Chambers (Moonie) outside the Talisman pub, Wolverhampton, in December 2001 in a drug-dealing dispute.
Key witnesses Lee Sellick, Carla Wedge, Carina Jackson and Donna Mills could not be found or gave statements through fear; Butterfield J allowed statements to be read under sections 23 and 26.
Tammy Pardoe gave hostile oral evidence; mobile phone and covert recording evidence supported the prosecution.
Witnesses entered witness protection then disappeared before trial amid intimidation linked to the defendants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder convictions on the ground that reading hearsay statements infringed Article 6(1) and 6(3)(d) ECHR.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions safe; discretion to read statements properly exercised with Schedule 2 counterbalancing and jury directions.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 does not create an absolute rule against reading sole or decisive hearsay where a witness is kept away by fear; where the defendant causes intimidation he cannot complain of inability to cross-examine, and sections 23/26 with section 28 safeguards and strong jury directions can preserve a fair trial.
legal_issues: Compatibility of sections 23 and 26 Criminal Justice Act 1988 with Article 6 ECHR
Whether statements were sole or decisive evidence against the appellants
Effect of witnesses being kept away through fear caused by defendants
Adequacy of counterbalancing procedures under section 28 and Schedule 2

confidence.notes: Extensive Strasbourg review, judge's rulings and Article 6 analysis support a confident enrichment.
